sections.heading: Path one: a foundation model of your own
Path two: when your data is not text

slides.title: Custom pretraining and *architecture*
slides.text: Your own model from scratch, or a different kind of model?

narration: At the top of the market, two very different things are sold in similar words.
This chapter helps you tell which one is in front of you.

slides.caption: Two different offers sit at the top of the market. This chapter shows how to tell them apart. It also shows whether either applies.

slides.title: What we will *cover*
items: How it links to the rest

narration: This is the last chapter of the ladder.
It is one of five ways to change the model itself.
Very few organisations ever need it.
First, we look at two offers that sound alike.
Then we look at path one.
That is building your own model from nothing.
Next is path two.
It is a different kind of model for data that is not text.
Last, we see how this links back to the rest of the ladder.

slides.caption: This last chapter covers two offers that sound alike. It explains building your own model and models for data that is not text. It ends with how both link back.

slides.title: What a *foundation model* is
slides.text: A large model that other work is built on.
slides.picture: One wide base block with smaller blocks built on top, beside a big stack of papers.

narration: Start with how most AI models are made.
They are trained on huge amounts of text from every subject.
Then other models and products are built on top of them.
A large model like this is called a foundation model.
Most teams start from one that someone else built.

slides.caption: A foundation model is a large model trained on huge amounts of text. Other work is built on top of it.

slides.title: Two things sold in *similar words*

right.head: A different kind of model
rows: For data that is not text

narration: Here are the two offers.
One is to build your own foundation model from nothing.
The other is a different kind of model.
It is built for data that is not text.
The first comes down to cost.
It is almost never the answer.
The second is real specialist work.
It has a clear use.

slides.caption: Path one is a cost decision that rarely pays. Path two is real specialist work for data like networks, sequences and signals.

slides.title: Path one: training *from scratch*

narration: Start with path one.
A model is a huge set of numbers.
Training slowly adjusts those numbers.
Here, the numbers start out random.
The model then reads trillions of small pieces of words.
This huge first training is called pretraining.
Nothing comes from an existing model.
So everything it knows must come from your own text.
Last, it is tuned so that people can use it.

slides.caption: Path one starts from random numbers and trains on trillions of word pieces. Everything the model knows comes from your own text.

slides.title: It needs a *top* AI lab's budget
slides.text: Computing power costing tens of millions, a research team, and time.
slides.picture: A very tall stack of coins beside a half-built model on a workbench and a large hourglass.

narration: Path one costs what only the biggest AI labs spend.
It needs computing power costing tens of millions and more.
It also needs a research team that stays in place.
Building takes a long time.
The field keeps moving while you build.
Meanwhile, open and paid models keep getting better.
Someone else pays for that.

slides.caption: Path one costs what the biggest AI labs spend. While you build, outside models keep improving on someone else's budget.

slides.title: When path one is *genuine*
items: A huge body of unusual text

narration: Path one does make sense in two cases.
In the first, a national rule bans using any model from outside.
This is called a sovereignty rule.
In the second, you hold a huge amount of text.
It is so unlike public text that existing models get it wrong.
This case also needs the money and the team.

slides.caption: Path one is genuine under a national sovereignty rule. It is also genuine with a huge body of text unlike public text, plus the money and team.

slides.title: First ask about continued *pretraining*
slides.text: What would it achieve on the same text?
slides.picture: A finished model taking in a stack of your own papers, with a heap of loose unbuilt parts set aside.

narration: One question settles most plans to build your own model.
What if you took an existing model and kept training it on your own text?
That is called continued pretraining.
It gives most of what people want from their own model.
It uses the same text.
It costs a small fraction as much.
And someone else keeps improving the model underneath.

slides.caption: Continued pretraining on the same text gives most of what people want from their own model. It costs far less. Someone else maintains the model underneath.

slides.title: If you do take *path one*
slides.text: A company's own study, using small models.

narration: If you do take path one, one finding may help.
It is about when to mix in text from your own field.
One study mixed a little of that text in from the very start.
That beat training on public text first and adding your text later.
The study was published by a company that sells help with training data.
It also used small models.
It can guide how you run path one.
It does not tell you whether to take it.

slides.caption: Mixing a little of your own text in from the start beat adding it later. It is a company's own study with small models. It guides how to run path one only.

slides.title: Path two: data that is *not text*
slides.picture: A web of linked records, a supply chain, a sensor signal line and a molecule, side by side.

narration: Now for path two.
The models on this ladder read text as a line of small word pieces.
Some data is not like that at all.
Think of records linked to each other, or supply chains.
Think of streams of sensor readings, or molecules.
None of this is a line of words.
None of the earlier steps on this ladder can change that.
Much of this data is things joined by links.
A set of things joined by links is called a graph.

slides.caption: Models that read text work on lines of word pieces. Networks, sensor streams and molecules are not like that. Things joined by links form a graph.

slides.title: A model built for *links*
slides.text: The most common one is a graph neural network.
slides.picture: A web of dots joined by lines, with a model facing it and a row of word bars set aside.

narration: For data like this, the model itself has to be different.
It has to learn from who is linked to whom.
The most common choice is called a graph neural network.
In this chapter, we just call it a graph model.

slides.caption: Data made of linked things needs a different kind of model. The most common is a graph neural network. We call it a graph model.

slides.title: Each thing is a *node*
slides.text: Each node starts with a list of numbers.
slides.picture: A web of dots joined by lines, with one dot carrying a small blank card of details.

narration: Here is how a graph model works, one step at a time.
Take one thing in the graph, such as one record.
It is called a node.
Each node starts with a list of numbers.
The numbers describe that one thing.

slides.caption: Each thing in a graph is called a node. Each node starts with a list of numbers that describe it.

slides.title: How a graph model *learns*

narration: Now the model gets to work.
It starts from each node's list of numbers.
A node's neighbours are the nodes it links to.
Each node updates its numbers using its neighbours' numbers.
One round of this is called a layer.
The model runs several layers, one after another.
After two layers, a node knows about its neighbours' neighbours.
Last, the model reads each node's numbers to make a prediction.
It learns from who connects to whom.
A model that reads documents cannot see that.

slides.caption: In each layer, nodes take in their neighbours' numbers. The model then reads each node's numbers to predict.

slides.title: Too many layers: nodes look *alike*
slides.picture: A cluster of differently coloured dots fading into one shared colour as layers stack up.

narration: This way of working has two known problems.
Each layer mixes a node's numbers with its neighbours' numbers.
Stack enough layers, and nearby nodes end up with the same numbers.
Then the model can no longer tell them apart.
This is called over-smoothing.
It is why graph models in real use often have only two or three layers.

slides.caption: Over-smoothing: with too many layers, nearby nodes end up alike. Graph models in real use often have only two or three layers.

slides.title: Far signals get *squashed*
slides.picture: Many distant dots funnelling through one narrow link into a single dot.

narration: The second problem pulls the other way.
Information from a far node must pass through many nodes to arrive.
The number of nodes on the way grows very fast with distance.
But each node holds only a fixed-size list of numbers.
So far information gets squeezed through narrow links.
Much of it is lost.
This is called over-squashing.

slides.caption: Over-squashing: information from far away is squeezed into fixed-size numbers. Much of it is lost at narrow links.

slides.title: The two problems pull *against* each other
slides.text: More layers ease over-squashing and worsen over-smoothing.

narration: So the two problems pull against each other.
More layers let information travel further.
That eases over-squashing.
But more layers make over-smoothing worse.
So turning one setting up does not fix both.
People who have really done this work change the design of the model.
A model's design is called its architecture.
Watch how someone handles this.
It shows whether they have real experience.

slides.caption: Adding layers eases over-squashing but worsens over-smoothing. Experienced people fix this by changing the design of the model.

slides.title: Three more problems to *listen for*
items: A huge graph must be cut

narration: There are three more problems worth listening for.
First, the learned numbers can stop being distinct.
Or learning can fade out in the deeper layers.
Then parts of the model quietly stop learning.
Second, a huge graph may not fit in memory.
So it must be cut into parts.
Every cut breaks real links.
So the model trains on a graph with links missing.
Third, the training may be spread across many machines.
Then training no longer behaves the way the textbooks describe.

slides.caption: Learned numbers can stop being distinct. Cutting a huge graph breaks real links. Training across many machines behaves differently.

slides.title: When path two is *genuine*
slides.text: You predict something about how things link, at real scale.
slides.picture: A wide web of identical dots with one small ring of links drawn in the accent colour.

narration: So when does path two make sense?
It fits when what you predict depends on how things link together.
It does not sit inside any one document.
The data must also be big enough for these problems to really matter.
This situation is easy to spot.
The rest of this ladder is about AI systems that carry out tasks.
These systems are called agents.
Path two has little to do with them.

slides.caption: Path two fits when the prediction depends on how things link. The data must be big enough for these problems to matter.

slides.title: The graph model is a *tool*
items: A tool passes score and evidence
Agent uses it in its draft

narration: Now, how does this connect back to agents?
The graph model is not the agent.
It does not chat.
It runs on its own as a scoring system.
That system has its own checks on whether the model can be trusted.
The agent reaches the score by asking a small program to fetch it.
A program like this is called a tool.
It returns the score and the part of the graph behind it.
The agent uses them as evidence in its draft.
A person makes the decision.

slides.caption: The graph model works out a score from the graph. A tool carries the score and its evidence to the agent. The agent drafts, and a person decides.

slides.title: Two teams that meet at a *tool*
slides.text: Different kinds of work, with different ways of managing risk.
slides.picture: Two separate workbenches, one with a web of dots and one with a model, joined by a single plug.

narration: This also means two different teams.
Every earlier step on this ladder starts from a model that already exists.
An engineering team builds around it.
The graph model needs a research team that builds models.
That team has its own way of checking and approving models.
These are two different kinds of work.
They meet at the tool.
Giving the graph model to the agent team is a mistake.
So is giving the agent to the graph team.

slides.caption: Every earlier step builds around an existing model. This chapter builds models. The two teams differ in budget, staff and risk checks. They meet at a tool.

slides.title: Try the *boring* options first

narration: Before building a custom graph model, try the simpler options.
First, work out a few simple measures of the graph by hand.
Then feed them to a simple model.
Second, try a ready-made graph model.
Keep it only a few layers deep.
Third, try rules for patterns you already know.
Each of these options gets a fair run first.

slides.caption: Before a custom model, try hand-made measures of the graph, a ready-made graph model, and rules for known patterns.

slides.title: The custom model must *beat* them
slides.text: Test on past cases with known right answers.

narration: Then compare them fairly.
Use past cases where you already know the right answer.
These are called labelled cases.
The custom model must beat the simple options on your own labelled cases.
This is the same fair test used at the start of this ladder.

slides.caption: The custom model must beat the simple options on your own labelled cases. It is the same fair test used earlier on this ladder.

slides.title: Diagnose the *failure* before you spend

narration: The same habit applies at every step of this ladder.
Find out what is really failing before you spend money.
Never assume a bigger version of what you have will fix it.

slides.caption: Find out what is really failing before spending. Never assume a bigger version of what you have will fix it.

slides.title: What to *remember*
items: The graph model is a tool

narration: Here is what to remember.
Building your own foundation model almost never pays.
First ask what continued pretraining on the same text would give.
Data made of linked things may need a graph model.
That model is a tool the agent calls.
A different team builds it.
At every step, find out what is failing before you spend.
The rule from the start of this ladder still holds.
Change the system before you change the model.

slides.caption: Building your own model rarely pays. Graph models suit data made of linked things. They work as tools. Change the system before you change the model.
